Global existence for the Einstein vacuum equations
in wave coordinates

Hans Lindblad   and Igor Rodnianski Thanks: Part of this work was done while H.L. was a Member of the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, supported by the NSF grant DMS-0111298 to the Institute. H.L. was also partially supported by the NSF Grant DMS-0200226. Thanks: Part of this work was done while I.R. was a Clay Mathematics Institute Long-Term Prize Fellow. His work was also partially supported by the NSF grant DMS–01007791. Affiliation: University of California at San Diego and Princeton University
Abstract

We prove global stability of Minkowski space for the Einstein vacuum equations in harmonic (wave) coordinate gauge for the set of restricted data coinciding with the Schwarzschild solution in the neighborhood of space-like infinity. The result contradicts previous beliefs that wave coordinates are ”unstable in the large” and provides an alternative approach to the stability problem originally solved ( for unrestricted data, in a different gauge and with a precise description of the asymptotic behavior at null infinity) by D. Christodoulou and S. Klainerman.

Using the wave coordinate gauge we recast the Einstein equations as a system of quasilinear wave equations and, in absence of the classical null condition, establish a small data global existence result. In our previous work we introduced the notion of a weak null condition and showed that the Einstein equations in harmonic coordinates satisfy this condition.The result of this paper relies on this observation and combines it with the vector field method based on the symmetries of the standard Minkowski space.

In a forthcoming paper we will address the question of stability of Minkowski space for the Einstein vacuum equations in wave coordinates for all ”small” asymptotically flat data and the case of the Einstein equations coupled to a scalar field.

1 Introduction

The focus of this paper is the question of global existence and stability for the Einstein vacuum equations in ”harmonic” (wave coordinate) gauge. The Einstein equations determine a 4-d manifold ℳ{\cal M} with a Lorentzian metric gg with vanishing Ricci curvature

Rμ​ν=0.R_{\mu\nu}=0.

We consider the initial value problem: for a given a 3-d manifold Σ\Sigma, with a Riemannian metric g0g_{0}, and a symmetric two-tensor k0k_{0}, we want to find a 4-d manifold ℳ{\cal M}, with a Lorentzian metric gg satisfying the Einstein equations, and an imbedding Σ⊂M\Sigma\subset M such that g0g_{0} is the restriction of gg to Σ\Sigma and k0k_{0} is the second fundamental form of Σ\Sigma in ℳ{\cal M}. The initial value problem is overdetermined which imposes compatibility conditions on the initial data: the constraint equations

R0−k0jik0ji+k0iik0jj=0,∇jk0i​j−∇ik0jj=0,∀i=1,…,3.R_{0}-{k_{0}}_{j}^{i}\,{k_{0}}^{j}_{i}+{k_{0}}_{i}^{i}\,{k_{0}}_{j}^{j}=0,\qquad\nabla^{j}{k_{0}}_{ij}-\nabla_{i}\,{k_{0}}_{j}^{j}=0,\qquad\forall i=1,...,3.

Here R0R_{0} is the scalar curvature of g0g_{0} and ∇\nabla is covariant differentiation with respect to g0g_{0}. The Einstein equations are invariant under diffeomorphisms. To have a working formulation one needs to eliminate this freedom by fixing a gauge condition or a system of coordinates.

While the Einstein equations are independent of the choice of a coordinate system, the existence of a special or preferred system of coordinates has been a subject of debate [Fo]. Historically, the first special coordinates were the harmonic coordinates (also referred to as wave coordinates in current terminology). These obey the equation □g​xμ=0\square_{g}\,x^{\mu}=0, μ=0,1,2,3\mu=0,1,2,3, where □g=∇α∇α\square_{g}=\nabla_{\alpha}\nabla^{\alpha} is the geometric wave operator. Relative to the wave coordinates a Lorentzian metric gg satisfies the wave coordinate condition if:11 1 We shall use below the standard convention of summing over repeated indices and the notation ∂α=∂/∂xα\partial_{\alpha}=\partial/\partial x^{\alpha}

(1.1) gα​β∂βgα​μ=12gα​β∂μgα​β,∀μ=0,..,3.g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\beta}g_{\alpha\mu}=\frac{1}{2}g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\mu}g_{\alpha\beta},\qquad\forall\mu=0,..,3.

In this system of coordinates, the vacuum Einstein equations take the form of a system of quasilinear wave equations

(1.2) gα​β​∂α∂βgμ​ν=𝒩μ​ν​(g,∂g),∀μ,ν=0,..,3g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}\,g_{\mu\nu}={\cal N}_{\mu\nu}(g,\partial g),\qquad\forall\mu,\nu=0,..,3

with a nonlinearity 𝒩⁡(u,v){\cal N}(u,v) depending quadratically on vv. In this particular gauge Choquet-Bruhat [CB1] was able to establish the existence of a globally hyperbolic development22 2 For the definitions of global hyperbolicity and maximal Cauchy development see [H-E], [Wa] of the Einstein vacuum equations starting with an arbitrary set of initial data prescribed on a 3-d space-like hypersurface and satisfying the constraint equations. While the result of Choquet-Bruhat and a later result of Choquet-Bruhat and Geroch [CB-G], establishing the existence of a maximal Cauchy development, constructs solutions for any given initial data set, it does not provide any information about the geodesic completeness of the obtained solution. In the language of the evolution equations these results only show the existence of ”local in time” solutions.

The global results have proved to be by far more resistant. The outstanding global problem, which for a long time remained open, and was finally ingeniously solved by Christodoulou and Klainerman [C-K], was that of the stability of Minkowski space. In simplified language, it is the problem of constructing a global solution to the Einstein vacuum equations from the initial data, which is close to the Minkowski metric mμ​νm_{\mu\nu}, and asymptotically approaching the Minkowski space. The initial data (Σ,g0,k0)(\Sigma,g_{0},k_{0}) for the problem of stability of Minkowski space is asymptotically flat, i.e., the complement of a compact set in Σ\Sigma is diffeomorphic to the complement of a ball in ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}, and there exists a system of coordinates (x1,x2,x3)(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3}) with r=x12+x22+x32r=\sqrt{x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2}} such that for all sufficiently large rr the metric33 3 The stability result of [C-K] was proved for strongly asymptotically flat data g0i​j=(1+2M/r)δi​j+o(r−3/2){g_{0}}_{ij}=(1+2M/r)\delta_{ij}+o(r^{-3/2}), k0=o(r−5/2)k_{0}=o(r^{-5/2}). g0i​j=(1+2​M/r)​δi​j+o⁡(r−1−σ){g_{0}}_{ij}=(1+2M/r)\delta_{ij}+o(r^{-1-\sigma}), and the second fundamental form k0=o⁡(r−2−σ)k_{0}=o(r^{-2-\sigma}) for some σ>0\sigma>0. Here MM is the mass, which by the positive mass theorem is positive unless the data is flat, see Schoen and Yau [S-Y] and Witten [Wi]. In addition, the data is required to satisfy a global smallness assumption, which makes sure that it is sufficiently close to the data (ℝ3,δ,0)({\mathbb{R}}^{3},\delta,0) for the Minkowski space.

To understand some of the difficulties of the problem we recall that a generic system of quasilinear equations

(1.3) □​ϕI=∑|α|≤|β|≤2AI,α​βJ​K​∂αϕJ​∂βϕK+cubic terms\square\phi_{I}=\sum_{|\alpha|\leq|\beta|\leq 2}A_{I,\alpha\beta}^{JK}\partial^{\alpha}\phi_{J}\partial^{\beta}\phi_{K}+{\text{cubic terms}}

allows solutions with smooth arbitrarily small initial data which blow up in finite time44 4 This is in particular true for a semilinear equation □​ϕ=(∂tϕ)2\square\phi=(\partial_{t}\phi)^{2}, [J1].. The key to global existence for such equations was the null condition found by Klainerman, [K2]. The small data global existence result for the equations satisfying the null condition was established in [C1], [K2]. The null condition manifests itself in special algebraic cancellations in the coefficients AI,α​βJ​KA_{I,\alpha\beta}^{JK} of the quadratic terms of the equation.55 5 E.g. □​ϕ=(∂tϕ)2−|∇xϕ|2\square\phi=(\partial_{t}\phi)^{2}-|\nabla_{x}\phi|^{2} satisfies the null-condition. It can be shown however, that the Einstein vacuum equations in wave coordinates do not satisfy the null condition. Moreover, Choquet-Bruhat [CB3] showed that even without imposing a specific gauge the Einstein equations violate the null condition.

These considerations led to the suggestion that the wave coordinates are not suitable for proving stability of Minkowski space. In fact, considering a second iterate of the equation (1.2), Choquet-Bruhat [CB2] argued that the Einstein vacuum equations are not stable in wave coordinates near the Minkowski solution. All these resulted in the belief that the wave coordinates are unstable in the large in the sense that a possible finite time blow up of solutions of the equation (1.2) is due to a coordinate singularity.

The global stability of Minkowski space had been proved by Christodoulou and Klainerman [C-K] who avoided the use of a preferred system of coordinates and instead relied on the invariant formulation of the Einstein equations with the choice of maximal time foliation (or the double null foliation in the new proof of Klainerman and Nicolo [K-N1]) and utilizing Bianchi identities for the curvature. The special structure of the quadratic terms plays a crucial part in the generalized energy estimates which form the backbone of the proof but the null condition can not be pointed out precisely.

A semiglobal stability result was also obtained in the work of Friedrich [Fr]. He used the conformal method to reduce the global problem to a local one. The approach is invariant and the special structure is again exploited implicitly.

In this paper we revisit the problem of global stability of Minkowski space in wave coordinates. More precisely, we consider the data66 6 The existence of such data is guaranteed by the results of Corvino and Chrusciel-Delay, [Co], [C-D]. (ℝ3,g0,k0)({\mathbb{R}}^{3},g_{0},k_{0}) with the metric g0g_{0} coinciding with the spatial part of the Schwarzschild metric gS=(1+M/r)4​d​x2g_{S}=(1+M/r)^{4}dx^{2} in the region r>1>>Mr>1>>M, vanishing second fundamental form k0k_{0} for r>1r>1, and satisfying a global smallness assumption on ℝ3{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. We prove that for this initial data the wave coordinate gauge is stable in the large: the reduced Einstein equations (1.2) has a global solution gg defining a future causally geodesically complete space-time, [H-E]. The metric gg in wave coordinates xα,α=0,..,3x^{\alpha},\,\alpha=0,..,3 approaches the Minkowski metric mm:   supx∈ℝ3|g⁡(t,x)−m|→0\sup_{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{3}}|g(t,x)-m|\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty.

The intuition behind this result is based on the observation that the Einstein vacuum equations in wave coordinates (1.2) satisfy the weak null condition. This notion was introduced in [L-R] for general quasilinear systems (1.3) and requires that the corresponding effective asymptotic system

(1.4) (∂t+∂r)(∂t−∂r)ΦI=r−1∑n≤m≤2AI,n​mJ​K(∂t−∂r)nΦJ(∂t−∂r)mΦK,ΦI∼rϕI(\partial_{t}+\partial_{r})(\partial_{t}-\partial_{r})\Phi_{I}={r}^{-1}\sum_{n\leq m\leq 2}A_{I,nm}^{JK}(\partial_{t}-\partial_{r})^{n}\Phi_{J}\,\,(\partial_{t}-\partial_{r})^{m}\Phi_{K},\qquad\Phi_{I}\sim r\phi_{I}

has global solutions for all small initial data.77 7 For the precise definition see section 6. Here,

AI,n​mJ​K​(ω)=∑|α|=n,|β|=mAI,α​βJ​K​ω^α​ω^β,ω^=(−1,ω),ω∈𝕊2.A_{I,nm}^{JK}(\omega)=\sum_{|\alpha|=n,|\beta|=m}A_{I,\alpha\beta}^{JK}\hat{\omega}^{\alpha}\hat{\omega}^{\beta},\qquad\hat{\omega}=(-1,\omega),\,\,\omega\in{\mathbb{S}}^{2}.

The classical null condition states that AI,n​mJ​K​(ω)≡0A_{I,nm}^{JK}(\omega)\equiv 0 and thus implies the weak null condition. The asymptotic system (1.4) arises as an approximation of (1.3) when one neglects the derivatives tangential to the outgoing Minkowski light cones, known to have faster decay. The asymptotic equation was introduced in [H1] to predict the time of a blow-up for scalar wave equations known to blow up in finite time, and was used in [L2] to find some other scalar wave equations for which the known blow-up mechanism was not present. Asymptotic systems played an important role in the analysis of the blow-up mechanisms in [A1].

In [L-R] we have shown that the asymptotic system generated by the Einstein equations in wave coordinates (1.2) has global solutions for all data. In this paper we consider the full nonlinear system (1.2). We should note that although the asymptotic system provides useful heuristics about the behavior of solutions, in particular the L∞L^{\infty} decay of the first derivatives of various components of the metric gg, it is barely used in our proof of the small data global existence result for the full nonlinear equation (1.2). While it is tempting to put forward a conjecture that, parallel to the result for the classical null condition [C1], [K2], the weak null condition guarantees the global existence result for small initial data, we can only argue that all known examples seem to confirm it. A simple example of an equation satisfying the weak null condition, violating the standard null condition and yet possessing global solutions for all data is given by the system

(1.5) □​ϕ=w⋅∂2ϕ+∂ψ⋅∂ψ,□​ψ=0,□​w=0\square\phi=w\cdot\partial^{2}\phi+\partial\psi\cdot\partial\psi,\qquad\quad\square\psi=0,\qquad\square w=0

Another example is provided by the equation □​ϕ=ϕ​Δ​ϕ\square\phi=\phi\Delta\phi. The proof of a small data global existence result for this equation is quite involved, [L2] (radial case), [A3]. As we show in this paper the Einstein equations (1.2) is yet another example. Interestingly enough, at the level of an effective asymptotic system the Einstein equations can be modelled by the system (1.5).

The asymptotic behavior of null components of the Riemann curvature tensor Rα​β​γ​δR_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} of metric gg- the so called ”peeling estimates”- was discussed in the works of Bondi, Sachs and Penrose and becomes important in the framework of asymptotically simple space-times (roughly speaking, space-times which can be conformally compactified), see also the paper of Christodoulou [C2] for further discussion of such space-times. Global solutions obtained in the work [C-K] were accompanied by very precise analysis of its asymptotic behavior although not entirely consistent with peeling estimates. However, global solutions obtained by Klainerman-Nicolo [K-N1] in the exterior88 8 Outside of the domain of dependence of a compact set stability of Minkowski space were shown to possess peeling estimates for special initial data, [K-N2].

Our work is less precise about the asymptotic behavior and is focused more on developing a technically relatively simple approach allowing us to prove stability of Minkowski space in a physically interesting wave coordinate gauge In particular, we rely only on the standard Killing and conformal Killing vector fields of Minkowski space and do not construct almost Killing and conformal Killing vector fields adapted to the geometry of null cones of the solution gg.

Our proof is based on generalized energy estimates combined with decay estimates. The generalized energy estimates are used with Minkowski vector fields {∂α,Ωα​β=xα∂β−xβ∂α,S=xα∂α}\{\partial_{\alpha},\Omega_{\alpha\beta}=x_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}-x_{\beta}\partial_{\alpha},S=x^{\alpha}\partial_{\alpha}\}. For the equations satisfying the standard null condition uniform in time bounds on the generalized energies, combined with global Sobolev (Klainerman-Sobolev) inequalities, are sufficient to infer small data global existence. In our case however the generalized energies slowly grow in time (at the rate of tεt^{\varepsilon}) and need to be complemented by independent, not following from the global Sobolev inequalities, decay estimates. We derive the latter by direct integration of the equation along the characteristics. It is at this point that the intuition from the effective asymptotic system is most useful. We show that all components of the metric with exception of one decay at the rate of t−1t^{-1}. The remaining component however decays only as t−1+εt^{-1+\varepsilon}. Somewhat surprisingly, the glue that holds together such weak decay estimates and the generalized energy estimates is the wave coordinate condition (1.1).

In this paper we only prove the result for a restricted set of data coinciding with the Schwarzschild data outside of the ball of radius one.99 9 Since the initial metric is always of the form gi​j=(1+4​M/r)​δi​j+o⁡(r−1)g_{ij}=(1+4M/r)\delta_{ij}+o(r^{-1}) with M>0M>0, data coinciding with the Schwarzschild outside of a compact set is the closest analogue of compactly supported or rapidly decaying data usually considered in small data global existence results for nonlinear wave equations. This allows us to somewhat sidestep the problem of a long range effect of a gravitational field. Due to the inward bending of the light rays, solution arising from initial data coinciding with the Schwarzschild data outside of the ball of radius one will be equal to the Schwarzschild solution in the exterior of the Minkowski cone r=t+1r=t+1.

In our subsequent work we hope to be able to prove the stability of Minkowski space in wave coordinates for general data. In addition we hope to show that our method can be also used to treat the problem of small data global existence for the Einstein equations coupled to a scalar field.

A corollary of the above result is the global stability of Minkowski space for a restricted set of initial data.

Theorem 2.3.

Let (ℝ3,g0,k0)({\mathbb{R}}^{3},g_{0},k_{0}) be the initial data set for the Einstein vacuum equations Rμ​ν=0R_{\mu\nu}=0. g0=(1+Mr)4​d​x2,r>1,g_{0}=(1+\frac{M}{r})^{4}dx^{2},\qquad r>1,

while the second fundamental form k0k_{0} vanishes for r>1r>1. In addition, we assume that relative to that system of coordinates g0g_{0}, MM and k0k_{0} satisfy the smallness condition

We now outline the strategy of the proof.

Remark 2.4.

Throughout the paper we shall use the notation A≲BA\lesssim B for the inequality A≤C​BA\leq CB with some large universal constant CC. In our estimates we will make no distinction between the tensors hα​β=gα​β−mα​βh_{\alpha\beta}=g_{\alpha\beta}-m_{\alpha\beta} and Hα​β=mα​α′​mβ​β′​(gα​β−mα​β)H_{\alpha\beta}=m_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}m_{\beta\beta^{\prime}}(g^{\alpha\beta}-m^{\alpha\beta}), since H=−h+O⁡(h2)H=-h+O(h^{2}) and the terms quadratic in hh are lower order.

The continuity argument For the proof we let δ\delta be any fixed number 0<δ<1/20<\delta<1/2. Let gg be a local smooth solution of the reduced Einstein equations (2.1). We start with the weak estimate

(2.6) EN​(t)≤64​ε2​(1+t)2​δE_{N}(t)\leq 64\varepsilon^{2}(1+t)^{2\delta}

It will then follow that the solution and the energy estimate (2.6) can be extended to a larger time interval [0,T′][0,T^{\prime}] thus contradicting the maximality of TT. The global Sobolev inequality of Proposition 9.2 and the weak energy estimate (2.6) imply the pointwise decay estimates:

(2.7) ∑|I|≤N−2|∂ZI​h​(t,x)|≤C​ε​(1+t)δ(1+t+r)​(1+|t−r|)1/2,r=|x|\sum_{|I|\leq N-2}|\partial Z^{I}h(t,x)|\leq\frac{C\varepsilon(1+t)^{\delta}}{(1+t+r)(1+|t-r|)^{1/2}},\qquad r=|x|

with some fixed constant γ>0\gamma>0. The weak decay estimates (2.8) will lead to much stronger decay estimates in Theorem 14.1. In turn, using the stronger decay estimates in Theorem 14.1 we will be able to obtain stronger energy estimates in Theorem 15.1, i.e. (2.5). These in particular will enable us to show that the estimate (2.6) holds globally in time and conclude the proof. We remark that in the course of the proof all constants will be independent of ε>0\varepsilon>0 but they will depend on a lower bound for γ>0\gamma>0 (and hence on an upper bound for δ<1/2\delta<1/2).

As described above, the proof is a direct consequence of three results. First is the global Sobolev inequality of Proposition 9.2, introduced by S. Klainerman [K1], giving decay estimates in terms of energy estimates for the generators of the Lorentz group. The second ingredient is the improved decay estimates in Theorem 14.1. The final component is the energy estimates in Theorem 15.1 which rely on the improved decay estimates.

Since the vector fields span the tangent space of the outgoing light cones r−t=qr-t=q we infer, with ∂¯\bar{\partial} denoting the derivatives tangential to the cones, that

(2.11) |∂¯ZIh|≲ε(1+r+t)−3/2−γ(1+|t−r|)1/2−γ,|\bar{\partial}Z^{I}h|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+r+t)^{-3/2-\gamma}(1+|t-r|)^{1/2-\gamma},

This means that, close to the light cone t=rt=r, derivatives tangential to the forward light cones decay quite a bit better than the expected decay rate from (2.8) for a generic derivative.

Wave coordinate condition. As we shall see below certain components of the tensor hh decay faster than others. This can be seen upon introduction of a null frame of vector fields L=∂t+∂rL=\partial_{t}+\partial_{r}, L¯=∂r−∂t\underline{L}=\partial_{r}-\partial_{t} and S1,S2S_{1},S_{2}: two orthonormal vectors tangential to the sphere of radius rr in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. The first improved estimates come from the wave coordinate condition (2.2). Writing gα​β=mα​β+hα​βg_{\alpha\beta}=m_{\alpha\beta}+h_{\alpha\beta} we obtain from (2.2) that

mα​β​∂αhβ​μ=∂μmα​β​hα​β+O⁡(h​∂h)m^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}h_{\beta\mu}=\partial_{\mu}m^{\alpha\beta}h_{\alpha\beta}+O(h\,\partial h)

In particular, contracting with a vector field T∈𝒯={L,S1,S2}T\in{\cal T}=\{L,S_{1},S_{2}\} and using that for any symmetric 2-tensor kk, mα​β​kα​β=−kL​L¯+δA​B​kA​Bm^{\alpha\beta}k_{\alpha\beta}=-k_{L\underline{L}}+\delta^{AB}k_{AB}, implies that we can express the transversal derivative ∂L¯\partial_{\underline{L}} of certain components of hh in terms of the tangential derivatives that decay better and a quadratic term

|(∂h)L​T|≤|∂¯​h|+|h|​|∂h|≲ε​(1+t+r)−1−2​γ,|hL​T|≲ε⁡(1+|t−r|)​(1+t+r)−1|(\partial h)_{LT}|\leq|\bar{\partial}h|+|h|\,|\partial h|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+t+r)^{-1-2\gamma},\qquad|h_{LT}|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+|t-r|)(1+t+r)^{-1}

Even though the estimate above does not give a better decay rate for all components of hh it gives the decay exactly for those components which, as it turns out, control the geometry, i.e., they lead to stronger energy and decay estimates.

The above estimates will be sufficient to obtain improved estimates for the lowest order energy of hh. However, in order to get estimates for the energy of ZI​hZ^{I}h we commute the vector fields ZZ through the equation for hh. This generates additional commutator terms. The main commutator terms are controlled with the help of the following additional estimate from the wave coordinate condition:

(2.12) |(∂h)L​T|+|(∂Z​h)L​L|≤ε​(1+t+r)−1−2​γ,|hL​T|+|(Z​h)L​L|≤ε⁡(1+|t−r|)​(1+t+r)−1|(\partial h)_{LT}|+|(\partial Zh)_{LL}|\leq\varepsilon(1+t+r)^{-1-2\gamma},\qquad|h_{LT}|+|(Zh)_{LL}|\leq\varepsilon(1+|t-r|)(1+t+r)^{-1}

We now describe derivation of the stronger decay and energy estimates.

Stronger decay estimates. We rely on the following decay estimate for the wave equation on a curved background 1212 12 Recall that the reduced wave operator □~g=gα​β∂2α​β\widetilde{\square}_{g}=g^{\alpha\beta}\partial^{2}_{\alpha\beta}.:

(2.13) ‖(1+t+r)​∂ϕ⁡(t,⋅)‖L∞≤C​∫0t(1+τ)​‖□~g​ϕ​(τ,⋅)‖L∞​𝑑τ+Csup0≤τ≤t∑|I|≤1∥ZIϕ(τ,⋅)∥L∞+C∫0t∑|I|≤2(1+τ)−1∥ZIϕ(τ,⋅)∥L∞dτ\|(1+t+r)\partial\phi(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}}\leq C\int_{0}^{t}(1+\tau)\|\widetilde{\square}_{g}\phi(\tau,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,d\tau\\ +C\sup_{0\leq\tau\leq t}\!\sum_{|I|\leq 1}\!\|Z^{I}\!\phi(\tau,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}}+C\int_{0}^{t}\sum_{|I|\leq 2}(1+\tau)^{-1}\|Z^{I}\phi(\tau,\cdot)\|_{L^{\infty}}\,d\tau

The estimate (2.13) will be applied to the components of the tensor hh. The term ZI​hZ^{I}h on the right hand side of the estimate will be controlled with the help of the weak decay estimates, and thus the decay rate of hh will be determined in terms of decay of □~g​h\widetilde{\square}_{g}h. The L∞−L∞L^{\infty}-L^{\infty} estimate (2.13) does not rely on the fundamental solution as does the more standard L1−L∞L^{1}-L^{\infty} type estimate. This estimate was used [L1] in the constant coefficient case and here we establish it in the variable coefficient case only under the assumption of the weak decay of all of the components of the metric gg and the stronger decay of the components of gg controlled by the wave coordinate condition. This analysis is by itself very interesting but we will not go into it here and just refer the reader to the following sections.

We now analyze the inhomogeneous term in the equation for hμ​νh_{\mu\nu}. The tensor hμ​ν=gμ​ν−mμ​νh_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}-m_{\mu\nu} verifies the reduced Einstein equations of the form:

□~g​hμ​ν=Fμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h),\displaystyle\widetilde{\square}_{g}h_{\mu\nu}=F_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h),
(2.14) Fμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h)=P⁡(∂μh,∂νh)+Qμ​ν​(∂h,∂h)+Gμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h),\displaystyle F_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h)=P(\partial_{\mu}h,\partial_{\nu}h)+Q_{\mu\nu}(\partial h,\partial h)+G_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h),
(2.15) P⁡(∂μh,∂νh)=14​∂μtr​h​∂νtr​h−12​∂μhα​β​∂νhα​β,\displaystyle P(\partial_{\mu}h,\partial_{\nu}h)=\frac{1}{4}\partial_{\mu}\text{tr}h\,\partial_{\nu}\text{tr}h-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\mu}h^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\nu}h_{\alpha\beta},

Here Qμ​νQ_{\mu\nu} are linear combinations of the standard null-forms and Gμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h)G_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h) is a quadratic form in ∂h\partial h with coefficients as smooth functions of hh vanishing at h=0h=0. The weak decay estimates imply that the last two terms decay fast

(2.16) |Qμ​ν​(∂h,∂h)|+|Gμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h)|≲|∂¯​h|​|∂h|+|h||∂h|2≲ε2​(1+r+t)−2−2​γ​(1+|t−r|)−2​γ|Q_{\mu\nu}(\partial h,\partial h)|+|G_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h)|\lesssim|\overline{\partial}h|\,|\partial h|+|h||\partial h|^{2}\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}(1+r+t)^{-2-2\gamma}(1+|t-r|)^{-2\gamma}

The problematic term is P⁡(∂μh,∂νh)P(\partial_{\mu}h,\partial_{\nu}h) since a priori the weak decay estimates only give the decay rate of ε2​(1+r+t)−1−2​γ​(1+|t−r|)−1−2​γ\varepsilon^{2}(1+r+t)^{-1-2\gamma}(1+|t-r|)^{-1-2\gamma}, which is not sufficient in the wave zone t≈rt\approx r. The crucial improvement comes as a result of a decomposition of the tensor P⁡(∂μh,∂νh)P(\partial_{\mu}h,\partial_{\nu}h) with respect to a null frame {L,L¯,S1,S2}\{L,\underline{L},S_{1},S_{2}\}. Let T∈𝒯={L,S1,S2}T\in{\cal T}=\{L,S_{1},S_{2}\} be any of the vectors generating the tangent space to the forward Minkowski light cones and U∈𝒰={L,L¯,S1,S2}U\in{\cal U}=\{L,\underline{L},S_{1},S_{2}\} denote any of the null frame vectors. Define, for an arbitrary symmetric two tensor kk, |k|𝒯𝒰=∑T∈𝒯,U∈𝒰=|TμUμkμ​ν||k|_{\cal TU}=\sum_{T\in{\cal T},U\in{\cal U}}=|T^{\mu}U^{\mu}k_{\mu\nu}|. It then follows that

(2.17) |P⁡(∂h,∂h)|𝒯𝒰≲|∂¯​h|​|∂h|≲ε2​(1+r+t)−2−2​γ​(1+|t−r|)−2​γ|P(\partial h,\partial h)|_{\cal TU}\lesssim|\overline{\partial}h|\,|\partial h|\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}(1+r+t)^{-2-2\gamma}(1+|t-r|)^{-2\gamma}

On the other hand, the absolute value of the tensor P⁡(∂h,∂h)P(\partial h,\partial h) obeys the estimate

(2.18) |P⁡(∂h,∂h)|≲|∂h|𝒯𝒰2+|​∂h|L​L​|∂h||P(\partial h,\partial h)|\lesssim|\partial h|_{\cal TU}^{2}+|\partial h|_{LL}|\partial h|

We now decompose the system of equations for hh with respect to the null-frame

(2.19) |□~g​h|𝒯𝒰\displaystyle|\widetilde{\square}_{g}h|_{\cal TU} ≲ε2​(1+r+t)−2−2​γ​(1+|t−r|)−2​γ,\displaystyle\lesssim\varepsilon^{2}(1+r+t)^{-2-2\gamma}(1+|t-r|)^{-2\gamma},
(2.20) |□~g​h|𝒰𝒰\displaystyle|\widetilde{\square}_{g}h|_{\cal UU} ≲|∂h|𝒯𝒰2+ε2​(1+r+t)−2−2​γ​(1+|t−r|)−2​γ,\displaystyle\lesssim|\partial h|_{\cal TU}^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}(1+r+t)^{-2-2\gamma}(1+|t-r|)^{-2\gamma},

where in the last inequality we also used the improved decay estimate for ∂hL​L\partial h_{LL} obtained from the wave coordinate condition. The result is a system of equations where the components □~g​hT​U\widetilde{\square}_{g}h_{TU} have very good decay properties, while □~g​hU​U\widetilde{\square}_{g}h_{UU} for the remaining non tangential component depends, to the highest order, only on the components hT​Uh_{TU} satisfying a better equation. An additional subtlety in the above analysis is the fact that contraction with the null frame does not commute with □~g\widetilde{\square}_{g} (or even with □\square). However, the decay estimate (2.13) for the wave equation only uses the principal radial part of □\square:  ∂t2−r−2∂r2−2r−1∂r\partial_{t}^{2}-r^{-2}\partial_{r}^{2}-2\,r^{-1}\partial_{r}, which respects the null frame. This analysis results in the improved decay estimates

(2.21) |∂h|T​U≤C​ε​(1+t)−1,|∂h|≤C​ε​(1+t)−1​ln⁡(2+t)|\partial h|_{TU}\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1},\qquad|\partial h|\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1}\ln(2+t)

The energy estimates. We rely on the following energy estimate for the wave equation, which holds under the assumption that the above decay estimates hold for the background metric gg: for any γ>0\gamma>0

(2.22) ∫ΣT|∂ϕ|2+∫0T∫Στγ​|∂¯​ϕ|2(1+|t−r|)1+2​γ≤8​∫Σ0|∂ϕ|2+C​ε​∫0T∫Σt|∂ϕ|21+t+16​∫0T∫Σt|□~g​ϕ|​|∂tϕ|\int_{\Sigma_{T}}|\partial\phi|^{2}+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Sigma_{\tau}}\frac{\gamma\,\,|\bar{\partial}\phi|^{2}}{(1+|t-r|)^{1+2\gamma}}\leq 8\int_{\Sigma_{0}}|\partial\phi|^{2}+C\varepsilon\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Sigma_{t}}\frac{|\partial\phi|^{2}}{1+t}+16\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\Sigma_{t}}|\widetilde{\square}_{g}\phi||\partial_{t}\phi|

This implies that the energy of a solution of the homogeneous wave equation □~g​ϕ=0\widetilde{\square}_{g}\phi=0 grows but at the rate of at most (1+t)C​ε(1+t)^{C\varepsilon}. The presence of an additional space-time integral containing tangential derivatives on the right and side of (2.22) is crucial for our analysis. This type of estimate in the constant coefficient case basically follows by averaging of the energy estimates on light cones used e.g. in [S1]. We also note that the energy estimates with space-time quantities involving special derivatives of a solution were also considered and used in the work of Alinhac, see e.g. [A2], [A3]). In our work we use the space-time integral with derivatives spanning the tangent space to outgoing light cones and weights dependent on the distance to the Minkowski light cone r=t+1r=t+1. We emphasize that the energy estimate (2.22) is proved only under the assumption of the weak decay of all components of the background metric gg together with the strong decay of the components controlled from the wave coordinate condition.

It is worth noting that a combination of the energy estimates of the type (2.22) and Klainerman-Sobolev inequalities would also yield a very simple proof of the small data global existence result for semilinear equations □​ϕ=Q⁡(∂ϕ,∂ϕ)\square\phi=Q(\partial\phi,\partial\phi) obeying the standard null condition. This fact appears to be previously unknown.

The energy estimate (2.22) will be applied simultaneously to all components of the tensor hh. As in the equations (2.19), (2.20) the inhomogeneous term obeys the following estimate:

|□~gh|≲ε(1+r+t)−3/2−γ(1+|t−r|)1/2−γ|∂h|+ε(1+t)−1|∂h|,|\widetilde{\square}_{g}h|\lesssim\varepsilon(1+r+t)^{-3/2-\gamma}(1+|t-r|)^{1/2-\gamma}|\partial h|+\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1}|\partial h|,

where in the last inequality we used the improved decay estimate for the |∂h|𝒯𝒰|\partial h|_{\cal TU} components. The energy estimate (11.3) will then imply that

E0​(t)≤16​ε2​(1+t)C​ε.E_{0}(t)\leq 16\varepsilon^{2}(1+t)^{C\varepsilon}.

Higher order energy estimates. In addition to the energy estimates for the components of the tensor hh we need estimates for the higher vector field derivatives of hh: ZI​hZ^{I}h with Minkowski vector fields Z={∂α,Ωα​β,S}Z=\{\partial_{\alpha},\Omega_{\alpha\beta},S\}. To obtain these estimates we apply ZIZ^{I} to the equation □~g​hμ​ν=Fμ​ν\widetilde{\square}_{g}h_{\mu\nu}=F_{\mu\nu} for hh. Applying vector fields to the nonlinear terms Fμ​νF_{\mu\nu} yields similar nonlinear terms for higher derivatives and these are can be dealt with using the estimates already described above. We must note however that this is where the additional space-time integral involving the tangential derivatives on the left hand side of the energy estimate (11.3) becomes crucial. Consider for example the term ∂h⋅∂¯​ZI​h\partial h\cdot\bar{\partial}Z^{I}h generated by one of the null forms in Fμ​νF_{\mu\nu}. We estimate its contribution, with the help of the weak decay estimates, to the energy estimate as follows:

|∂h​‖∂¯​ZI​h‖​∂tZI​h|≤C​ε​|∂tZI​h|(1+t)1/2+γ​|∂¯​ZI​h|(1+|t−r|)1/2+γ≤C​ε​|∂tZI​h|2(1+t)1+2​γ+C​ε​|∂¯​ZI​h|2(1+|t−r|)1+2​γ|\partial h|\,|\bar{\partial}Z^{I}h||\partial_{t}Z^{I}h|\leq\frac{C\varepsilon|\partial_{t}Z^{I}h|}{(1+t)^{1/2+\gamma}}\frac{|\bar{\partial}Z^{I}h|}{(1+|t-r|)^{1/2+\gamma}}\leq\frac{C\varepsilon|\partial_{t}Z^{I}h|^{2}}{(1+t)^{1+2\gamma}}+\frac{C\varepsilon|\bar{\partial}Z^{I}h|^{2}}{(1+|t-r|)^{1+2\gamma}}

The integral of the first term is easily controlled by the energy on time slices times an integrable factor in time. The space time integral of the second term is in fact part of the energy (2.22), and if we choose ε\varepsilon sufficiently small this term can be absorbed by the space time integral on the left. The idea with the space-time integral is that one can use the extra decay in |t−r||t-r| when one does not have full decay in tt.

The more serious problem in higher order energy estimates lies however in the commutators between ZIZ^{I} and the principal part □~g=gα​β∂α∂β\widetilde{\square}_{g}=g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}.

The commutators. Writing gα​β=mα​β+Hα​βg^{\alpha\beta}=m^{\alpha\beta}+H^{\alpha\beta} with Hα​β=−mα​α′​mβ​β′​hα′​β′+O⁡(h2)H^{\alpha\beta}=-m^{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}m^{\beta\beta^{\prime}}h_{\alpha^{\prime}\beta^{\prime}}+O(h^{2}), we show the following commutator estimate1313 13 This commutator estimate applies to the vector fields Z={∂α,Ωα​β}Z=\{\partial_{\alpha},\Omega_{\alpha\beta}\}. For the scaling vector field Z=S=xα∂αZ=S=x^{\alpha}\partial_{\alpha} the commutator expression should have the form □~g​S−(S+2)​□~g\widetilde{\square}_{g}S-(S+2)\widetilde{\square}_{g} .

(2.23) |[Z,□~g]​ϕ|≤C⁡(|H|+|Z​H|1+t+r+|Z​H|L​L+|H|L​𝒯1+|t−r|)​∑|I|≤1|∂ZI​ϕ|≤C​ε1+t+r​∑|I|≤1|∂ZI​ϕ|\big|[Z,\widetilde{\square}_{g}]\phi\big|\leq C\Big(\frac{|H|+|ZH|}{1+t+r}+\frac{|ZH|_{LL}+|H|_{L\cal T}}{1+|\,t-r|}\Big)\sum_{|I|\leq 1}|\partial Z^{I}\phi|\leq\frac{C\varepsilon}{1+t+r}\sum_{|I|\leq 1}|\partial Z^{I}\phi|

by the weak decay assumptions (2.10) and the improved decay from the wave coordinate condition (2.12). We should note that for a generic quasilinear wave equation commutators with Minkowski vector fields ZZ give rise to uncontrollable error terms. In the special case of the equation □​ϕ=ϕ​Δ​ϕ\square\phi=\phi\Delta\phi this problem can be overcome by modifying the vector fields ZZ, [A3]. In our case it is the wave coordinate gauge that provides additional cancellations.

This commutator estimate applied to ϕ=hα​β\phi=h_{\alpha\beta} together with the analysis in the previous section now gives estimates for the energy E1E_{1} as well as for the stronger decay estimates for the second derivatives of hh, (2.26) with |J|=1|J|=1. This commutator will also show up as a top order term [Z,□~g]⋅ZI−1​hα​β[Z,\widetilde{\square}_{g}]\cdot Z^{I-1}h_{\alpha\beta} in the energy estimate for ZI​hZ^{I}h and the resulting term can be dealt with in the same way.

The other top order term generated by the commutators [ZI,□~g]​ϕ[Z^{I},\widetilde{\square}_{g}]\phi is of the form (ZIHα​β)∂α∂β(Z^{I}H^{\alpha\beta})\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}. We first apply the pointwise estimate

|(ZI​Hα​β)​∂α∂βϕ|≤C⁡(|ZI​H|1+t+r+|ZI​H|L​L1+|t−r|)​∑|K|≤1|∂ZK​ϕ||(Z^{I}H^{\alpha\beta})\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}\phi|\leq C\Big(\frac{|Z^{I}H|}{1+t+r}+\frac{|Z^{I}H|_{LL}}{1+|\,t-r|}\Big)\sum_{|K|\leq 1}|\partial Z^{K}\phi|

To deal with its contribution to the energy estimate we use the Poincare estimate with a boundary term

(2.24) ∫R3|ZI​H|L​L2​d​x(1+|t−r|)2+2​σ≤C∫S(t+1)|ZIH|L​L2dS+C∫R3|∂rZI​H|L​L2​d​x(1+|t−r|)2​σ,σ>−1/2,σ≠1/2\int\limits_{R^{3}}\frac{|Z^{I}H|_{LL}^{2}\,dx}{(1+|t-r|)^{2+2\sigma}}\leq C\int\limits_{S_{(t+1)}}|Z^{I}H|_{LL}^{2}\,dS+C\int\limits_{R^{3}}\frac{|\partial_{r}Z^{I}H|_{LL}^{2}\,dx}{(1+|t-r|)^{2\sigma}},\qquad\sigma>-1/2,\quad\sigma\neq 1/2

together with the fact that hh is Schwarzschild outside the cone r=t+1r=t+1, because of the inward bending of the Schwarzschild light cones, and hence there |ZI​h|≤C​ε/(1+t)|Z^{I}h|\leq C\varepsilon/(1+t). The way coordinate condition implies that |∂ZI​H|L​L|\partial Z^{I}H|_{LL} can be estimated by |∂¯​ZI​H||\bar{\partial}Z^{I}H| and lower order terms. The term involving |∂¯​ZI​H||\bar{\partial}Z^{I}H| is then controlled by the space-time integral on the left hand side.

One can use a similar but more trivial argument for decay estimates, i.e.

|ZI​H|L​L≤|ZI​HL​L|r=t+1+(1+|t−r|)​|∂rZI​HL​L|L∞|Z^{I}H|_{LL}\leq{|Z^{I}H_{LL}|}_{r=t+1}+(1+|t-r|){|\partial_{r}Z^{I}H_{LL}|}_{L^{\infty}}

The lower order terms. So far we have only discussed the top order terms, but there will also be several lower order terms (relative to |I|=k+1|I|=k+1) to deal with. These are typically of the form

(2.25) |∂ZJ​h|​|∂ZK​h|or|ZJ​h|​|∂2ZK−1​h|≤C​|ZJ​h|1+|t−r|​|∂ZK​h||\partial Z^{J}h|\,|\partial Z^{K}h|\qquad\text{or}\qquad|Z^{J}h|\,|\partial^{2}Z^{K-1}h|\leq C\frac{|Z^{J}h|}{1+|t-r|}\,|\partial Z^{K}h|

(2.27) M⁡(t)≤∫0tC​ε​M​(s)1+s+C​ε2(1+s)1−C​ε​𝑑sM(t)\leq\int_{0}^{t}\frac{C\varepsilon\,M(s)}{1+s}\,+\frac{C\varepsilon^{2}}{(1+s)^{1-C\varepsilon}}\,ds

3 The Einstein equations in wave coordinates

For a Lorentzian metric gμ​νg_{\mu\nu}, where μ,ν=0,…,3\mu,\nu=0,...,3 we denote

(3.1) Γμ​νλ=12​gλ​δ​(∂μgδ​ν+∂νgδ​μ−∂δgμ​ν),\Gamma_{\mu\,\,\,\nu}^{\,\,\,\lambda}=\frac{1}{2}g^{\lambda\delta}\big(\partial_{\mu}g_{\delta\nu}+\partial_{\nu}g_{\delta\mu}-\partial_{\delta}g_{\mu\nu}\big),

the Christoffel symbols of gg and

(3.2) Rμ​ν​δλ=∂δΓμ​νλ−∂νΓμ​δλ+Γρ​δλ​Γμ​νρ−Γρ​νλ​Γμ​δρR_{\mu\,\,\,\nu\delta}^{\,\,\,\lambda}=\partial_{\delta}\Gamma_{\mu\,\,\,\nu}^{\,\,\,\lambda}-\partial_{\nu}\Gamma_{\mu\,\,\,\delta}^{\,\,\,\lambda}+\Gamma_{\rho\,\,\,\delta}^{\,\,\,\lambda}\Gamma_{\mu\,\,\,\nu}^{\,\,\,\rho}-\Gamma_{\rho\,\,\,\nu}^{\,\,\,\lambda}\Gamma_{\mu\,\,\,\delta}^{\,\,\,\rho}

its Riemann curvature tensor with Rμ​ν=Rμ​ν​ααR_{\mu\nu}=R_{\mu\,\,\,\nu\alpha}^{\,\,\,\alpha}, the Ricci tensor.

We consider the metric gg satisfying the Einstein vacuum equations

(3.3) Rμ​ν=0.R_{\mu\nu}=0.

We impose the wave coordinate condition:

(3.4) Γλ:=gα​β​Γα​βλ=0\Gamma^{\lambda}:=g^{\alpha\beta}\,\Gamma_{\alpha\,\,\,\beta}^{\,\,\,\lambda}=0

It follows that assuming (3.4) we have that the reduced wave operator □~g=gα​β\widetilde{\square}_{g}=g^{\alpha\beta}

(3.5) □~g=□g=1|g|∂αgα​β|g|∂β\widetilde{\square}_{g}={\square}_{g}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|g|}}\partial_{\alpha}g^{\alpha\beta}\sqrt{|g|}\partial_{\beta}

The following lemma provides the description of the Einstein vacuum equations in wave coordinates as a system of quasilinear wave equations for gμ​νg_{\mu\nu}.

Lemma 3.1.

Let metric gg satisfy the Einstein vacuum equations (3.3) together with the wave coordinate condition (3.4). Then gμ​νg_{\mu\nu} solves the following system of reduced Einstein equations:

(3.6) □~g​gμ​ν=P~​(∂μg,∂νg)+Q~μ​ν​(∂g,∂g){\widetilde{\square}}_{g}g_{\mu\nu}=\widetilde{P}(\partial_{\mu}g,\partial_{\nu}g)+\widetilde{Q}_{\mu\nu}(\partial g,\partial g)

(3.22) mα​β​∂αhβ​μ=12​mα​β​∂μhα​β+Gμ​(h)​(∂h),or∂αHα​ν=12​gα​β​(mν​μ+Hν​μ)​∂μHα​βm^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}h_{\beta\mu}=\frac{1}{2}m^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\mu}h_{\alpha\beta}+G_{\mu}(h)(\partial h),\qquad\text{or}\qquad\partial_{\alpha}H^{\alpha\nu}=\frac{1}{2}g_{\alpha\beta}\big(m^{\nu\mu}+H^{\nu\mu}\big)\partial_{\mu}H^{\alpha\beta}

where Gμ​(h)​(∂h)G_{\mu}(h)(\partial h) is a linear function of ∂h\partial h with coefficients that are smooth functions of hh and that vanishes when hh vanishes: Gμ​(0)​(∂h)=0G_{\mu}(0)(\partial h)=0.

Observe that the terms in (3.20) do not satisfy the classical null condition. However the trace mμ​ν​hμ​νm^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu} satisfies a nonlinear wave equation with semilinear terms obeying the the null condition:

gα​β​∂α∂βmμ​ν​hμ​ν=Q⁡(∂h,∂h)+G⁡(h)​(∂h,∂h).g^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}m^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\nu}=Q(\partial h,\partial h)+G(h)(\partial h,\partial h).

4 The initial data

In this section we discuss the initial data for which the results of our paper apply. We shall consider the asymptotically flat data, satisfying a global smallness condition, with the property that it coincides with the Schwarzschild data outside the ball of radius one.

We start by showing the existence of such data. Let (g0,k0)(g_{0},k_{0}) be asymptotically flat initial data for the Einstein equations consisting of the Riemannian metric g0g_{0} and a second fundamental form k0k_{0}. The initial data for the vacuum Einstein satisfy the constraint equations

(4.1) R0−(tr​k0)2+|k0|2=0,\displaystyle R_{0}-(\text{tr}k_{0})^{2}+|k_{0}|^{2}=0,
(4.2) ∇jk0i​j−∇itr​k0=0\displaystyle\nabla^{j}{k_{0}}_{ij}-\nabla_{i}\text{tr}k_{0}=0

We restrict our attention to the time-symmetric case R0=k0=0R_{0}=k_{0}=0. Then, if (g0,k0)(g_{0},k_{0}) is sufficiently close to the Minkowski data and g0g_{0} satisfies the parity condition g0​(x)=g0​(−x)g_{0}(x)=g_{0}(-x), by the results of Corvino [Co] and Chrusciel-Delay [C-D] one can construct a new set of initial data (g,k)(g,k) with the properties that

  • •

    The initial data (g,k)(g,k) coincides with (g0,k0)(g_{0},k_{0}) on the ball of radius 1/2.

  • •

    (g,k)(g,k) is exactly the Schwarzschild data (gSx,0)(g_{S}^{x},0) of mass MM outside B1B_{1}, the ball of radius one.

At this point we specify the smallness conditions:

(4.3) M≤ϵ,∑0≤|I|≤N(‖∂xI(g−δ)‖L2​(B1)+∑0≤|J|≤N−1‖∂xJk‖L2​(B1))≤ϵM\leq\epsilon,\qquad\sum_{0\leq|I|\leq N}\Big(\|\partial_{x}^{I}(g-\delta)\|_{L^{2}(B_{1})}+\sum_{0\leq|J|\leq N-1}\|\partial^{J}_{x}k\|_{L^{2}(B_{1})}\Big)\leq\epsilon

for some sufficiently large integer NN. Here ∂xI\partial_{x}^{I} denotes the derivative ∂x1I1…∂xnIn\partial_{x_{1}}^{I_{1}}...\partial_{x_{n}}^{I_{n}}, where (I1,..,In)(I_{1},..,I_{n}) is an arbitrary multi-index with the property that I1+..+In=|I|I_{1}+..+I_{n}=|I|.

We have two expressions for the Schwarzschild metric in isotropic and wave coordinates:

(4.4) gS=−(1−M/r)2(1+M/r)2​d​t2+(1+Mr)4​d​x2,\displaystyle g_{S}=-\frac{(1-M/{r})^{2}}{(1+M/{r})^{2}}dt^{2}+(1+\frac{M}{r})^{4}dx^{2},
(4.5) gs=−r−2​Mr+2​M​d​t2+r+2​Mr−2​M​d​r2+(r+2​M)2​(d​θ2+sin2⁡θ​d​ϕ2)\displaystyle g_{s}=-\frac{r-2M}{r+2M}dt^{2}+\frac{r+2M}{r-2M}dr^{2}+(r+2M)^{2}(d\theta^{2}+\sin^{2}\theta d\phi^{2})

The expressions gSxg_{S}^{x} and gsxg_{s}^{x} will denote the spatial parts the Schwarzschild metric in respective coordinates. Observe that

(4.6) gs=m+4​Mr​(d​t2+d​x2)+O⁡(r−2),g_{s}=m+\frac{4M}{r}(dt^{2}+dx^{2})+O(r^{-2}),

We now find the coordinate change transforming the metric gSg_{S} into gsg_{s}. Set

(4.7) t=τ,r=ρ+M2ρt=\tau,\qquad r=\rho+\frac{M^{2}}{\rho}

In the coordinates τ,ρ\tau,\rho the metric gsg_{s} takes the form gSg_{S}. This change of coordinates is one-to-one for the values ρ>M\rho>M. Since the mass M<<1M<<1 we can define the change of coordinates r=Φ⁡(ρ)r=\Phi(\rho), where Φ\Phi coincides with the map (4.7) for ρ>1\rho>1 and the identity transformation for ρ≤1/2\rho\leq 1/2. Thus we have constructed the initial data (g,k)(g,k) such that

  • •

    The initial data (g,k)(g,k) coincides (in new coordinates) with (g0,k0)(g_{0},k_{0}) on the ball of radius 1/2.

  • •

    (g,k)(g,k) is exactly the Schwarzschild data (gsx,0)(g^{x}_{s},0) outside the ball of radius one.

  • •

    Moreover, the new data still obeys the smallness condition (4.3).

The constructed metric is already in wave coordinates on its Schwarzschild part. We now describe the procedure which produces the initial data (g,∂tg)(g,\partial_{t}g) associated with (g,k)(g,k) and satisfying the wave coordinate condition.

Recall that a priori we are only given the spatial part of the metric gi​jg_{ij} together with a second fundamental form ki​jk_{ij}. We now define the full space-time metric gα​βg_{\alpha\beta} on the Cauchy hypersurface Σ0\Sigma_{0} as follows:

(4.8) g0​i=0,g00=−a⁡(r),g_{0i}=0,\qquad g_{00}=-a(r),

where the function

a⁡(r)=r−2​Mr+2​M,for​r>1\displaystyle a(r)=\frac{r-2M}{r+2M},\qquad{\text{for}}\,\,\,r>1
a⁡(r)=1,for​r≤12\displaystyle a(r)=1,\qquad{\text{for}}\,\,\,r\leq\frac{1}{2}

Thus defined metric coincides with the full Schwarzschild metric gsg_{s} for r>1r>1. We further define

(4.9) ∂tgi​j=−2​a​ki​j\partial_{t}g_{ij}=-2ak_{ij}

It remains to determine ∂tg0​α\partial_{t}g_{0\alpha}. We find it by satisfying the wave coordinate condition

gβ​μ​∂μgα​β=12​gμ​ν​∂αgμ​νg^{\beta\mu}\partial_{\mu}g_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{\alpha}g_{\mu\nu}

Setting α=0\alpha=0 we obtain

12g00∂tg00=−gβ​i∂ig0​β+12gi​j∂tgi​j\frac{1}{2}g^{00}\partial_{t}g_{00}=-g^{\beta i}\partial_{i}g_{0\beta}+\frac{1}{2}g^{{ij}}\partial_{t}g_{ij}

This defines ∂tg00\partial_{t}g_{00}. On the other hand setting α=i\alpha=i we obtain

g00∂tg0​i=−gβ​j∂jgi​β+12gμ​ν∂igμ​νg^{00}\partial_{t}g_{0i}=-g^{\beta j}\partial_{j}g_{i\beta}+\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu\nu}\partial_{i}g_{\mu\nu}

This determines ∂tg0​i\partial_{t}g_{0i}. Observe that since the metric gg coincides with the Schwarzschild metric gsg_{s}, already satisfying the wave coordinate condition, outside the ball of radius one, we have that on that set the initial data takes the form (gs,0)(g_{s},0). Hence we constructed the initial data (g,∂tg)(g,\partial_{t}g) with the properties that

  • •

    The initial data (g,∂tg)(g,\partial_{t}g) corresponds to the initial data (g,k)(g,k) prescribed originally.

  • •

    (g,∂tg)(g,\partial_{t}g) is exactly the Schwarzschild data (gs,0)(g_{s},0) outside the ball of radius one.

  • •

    The initial data verifies the wave coordinate condition.

  • •

    The initial data satisfies the smallness condition

    (4.10) ∑0≤|I|≤N(‖∂xI(g−m)‖L2​(B1)+∑0≤|J|≤N−1‖∂xJ∂tg‖L2​(B1))≤ϵ\sum_{0\leq|I|\leq N}\Big(\|\partial_{x}^{I}(g-m)\|_{L^{2}(B_{1})}+\sum_{0\leq|J|\leq N-1}\|\partial^{J}_{x}\partial_{t}g\|_{L^{2}(B_{1})}\Big)\leq\epsilon

Now with the initial data (g,∂tg)(g,\partial_{t}g) we solve the reduced Einstein equations (3.6). It follows from the proof of Lemma 3.1 that, in the notation Γλ=gα​β​Γα​βλ\Gamma^{\lambda}=g^{\alpha\beta}\Gamma^{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}, the reduced Einstein equations can be written in the form:

(4.11) 𝐑α​β−12​(Dα​Γβ+Dβ​Γα)−Γσ​Nα​βσ​(g,∂g)=0.{\bf{R}}_{\alpha\beta}-\frac{1}{2}(D_{\alpha}\Gamma_{\beta}+D_{\beta}\Gamma_{\alpha})-\Gamma_{\sigma}N^{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta}(g,\partial g)=0.

Here DD denotes a covariant derivative with respect to the space-time metric gg and Nα​βσN^{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta} are some given functions depending on gg and ∂g\partial g. Observe that the initial data (g,∂tg)(g,\partial_{t}g) were chosen in such a way that the wave coordinate condition Γλ=0\Gamma^{\lambda}=0 is satisfied on the initial hypersurface Σ0\Sigma_{0}. We now argue that this condition is propagated, i.e, the solution of the reduced Einstein equations (4.11) obeys Γλ=0\Gamma^{\lambda}=0 on any hypersuface Σt\Sigma_{t}. We would have thus shown that a solution of the reduced Einstein equations is, in fact, a solution of the vacuum Einstein equations.

To prove that Γλ=0\Gamma^{\lambda}=0 we differentiate (4.11) and use the contracted Bianchi identity Dβ​𝐑α​β=12​Dα​𝐑D^{\beta}{\bf{R}}_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{1}{2}D_{\alpha}{\bf{R}}

0\displaystyle 0 =2​(Dβ​𝐑α​β−12​Dα​𝐑)=Dβ​Dα​Γβ+Dβ​Dβ​Γα−Dα​Dβ​Γβ−2​Dβ​(Γσ​Nα​βσ)−Dα​(Γσ​Nβσ​β)\displaystyle=2(D^{\beta}{\bf{R}}_{\alpha\beta}-\frac{1}{2}D_{\alpha}{\bf{R}})=D^{\beta}D_{\alpha}\Gamma_{\beta}+D^{\beta}D_{\beta}\Gamma_{\alpha}-D_{\alpha}D^{\beta}\Gamma_{\beta}-2D^{\beta}(\Gamma_{\sigma}N^{\sigma}_{\alpha\beta})-D_{\alpha}(\Gamma_{\sigma}N^{\sigma\beta}_{\beta})
=Dβ​Dβ​Γα+𝐑α​γ​Γγ−2​(Dβ​Γσ)​Nβσ​β−(Dα​Γσ)​Nβσ​β−2​Γσ​(Dβ​Nασ​β)−Γσ​(Dα​Nβσ​β)\displaystyle=D^{\beta}D_{\beta}\Gamma_{\alpha}+{\bf{R}}_{\alpha\gamma}\Gamma^{\gamma}-2(D_{\beta}\Gamma_{\sigma})N^{\sigma\beta}_{\beta}-(D_{\alpha}\Gamma_{\sigma})N^{\sigma\beta}_{\beta}-2\Gamma_{\sigma}(D_{\beta}N^{\sigma\beta}_{\alpha})-\Gamma_{\sigma}(D_{\alpha}N^{\sigma\beta}_{\beta})

Therefore, Γλ\Gamma^{\lambda} satisfies a covariant wave equation, on the background determined by the constructed metric gg, with the initial condition Γλ=0\Gamma^{\lambda}=0. It remains to show that Dt​Γλ=0D_{t}\Gamma^{\lambda}=0 on Σ0\Sigma_{0} and the conclusion that Γλ≡0\Gamma^{\lambda}\equiv 0 will follows by the uniqueness result for wave equation.

We recall that the initial data (g,k)(g,k) verifies the constraint equations (4.1), (4.2), which imply that on Σ0\Sigma_{0}

𝐑T​T+12​𝐑=0,𝐑T​i=0,{\bf{R}}_{TT}+\frac{1}{2}{\bf{R}}=0,\qquad{\bf{R}}_{Ti}=0,

where T=−(g00)−1∂tT=-(g_{00})^{-1}\partial_{t} is the unit future oriented normal to Σ0\Sigma_{0}. Therefore returning to (4.11) we obtain that

0=𝐑00+12​𝐑=−(g00)−1​Dt​Γ0+Di​Γi,\displaystyle 0={\bf{R}}_{00}+\frac{1}{2}{\bf{R}}=-(g_{00})^{-1}D_{t}\Gamma_{0}+D^{i}\Gamma_{i},
0=𝐑0​i=12​Dt​Γi+12​Di​Γ0\displaystyle 0={\bf{R}}_{0i}=\frac{1}{2}D_{t}\Gamma_{i}+\frac{1}{2}D_{i}\Gamma_{0}

This finishes the proof that Γλ≡0\Gamma^{\lambda}\equiv 0.

We also know that the time-independent Schwarzschild metric gsg_{s} is a solution of the Einstein vacuum equation 𝐑α​β=0{\bf{R}}_{\alpha\beta}=0. Moreover, since gsg_{s} satisfies the wave coordinate condition it also verifies the reduced Einstein equations (4.11). Since the initial data (g,∂tg)=(gs,0)(g,\partial_{t}g)=(g_{s},0) outside the ball of radius two, constructed solution will coincide with the Schwarzschild solution in the exterior of the null cone developed from the sphere of radius one in Σ0\Sigma_{0}.

We end the discussion of the initial data by comparing the light cones of Minkowski and Schwarzschild spaces in the wave coordinates of the Schwarzschild space.

Lemma 4.1.

For an arbitrary R>2​MR>2M the forward null cone of the metric gsg_{s}, intersecting the time slice t=0t=0 along the sphere of radius RR, is contained in the interior of the Minkowski cone t−r=Rt-r=R.

Proof.

The null cone intersecting the time slice t=0t=0 along the sphere of radius RR can be realized as the level hypersurface u=0u=0 of the optical function uu solving the eikonal equation

gsα​β​∂αu​∂βu=0g_{s}^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}u\,\,\partial_{\beta}u=0

with the initial condition that u=0u=0 on the sphere of radius RR at time t=0t=0. Because of the spherical symmetry of the Schwarzschild metric gsg_{s} and the initial condition we look for a spherically symmetric solution u=u⁡(t,r)u=u(t,r). The eikonal equation then reads

r+2​Mr−2​M​(∂tu)2=r−2​Mr+2​M​(∂ru)2\frac{r+2M}{r-2M}(\partial_{t}u)^{2}=\frac{r-2M}{r+2M}(\partial_{r}u)^{2}

Let t=γ⁡(r)t=\gamma(r) be a null geodesic, originating from some point on the sphere of radius RR at t=0t=0, such that u⁡(γ⁡(r),r)=0u(\gamma(r),r)=0. Then

∂tu​γ˙​(r)+∂ru=0\partial_{t}u\dot{\gamma}(r)+\partial_{r}u=0

Substituting this into the eikonal equation we obtain that

(r+2​Mr−2​M)2=|γ˙​(r)|2\Big(\frac{r+2M}{r-2M}\Big)^{2}=|\dot{\gamma}(r)|^{2}

Taking the square root and integrating we obtain that

γ⁡(r)=γ⁡(R)±(r−R+4​M​ln⁡r−2​MR−2​M)\gamma(r)=\gamma(R)\pm\Big(r-R+4M\ln\frac{r-2M}{R-2M}\Big)

Thus the null geodesics are described the curves

t=±(r−R+4​M​ln⁡r−2​MR−2​M)t=\pm\Big(r-R+4M\ln\frac{r-2M}{R-2M}\Big)

In particular, the forward null cone is contained in the interior of the set t≥r−Rt\geq r-R. ∎

5 The null-frame and null-forms

Below we introduce a standard Minkowski null-frame used throughout the paper. At each point (t,x)(t,x) we introduce a pair of null vectors (L,L¯)(L,\underline{L})

L0=1,Li=xi/|x|,i=1,2,3,andL¯0=1,L¯i=−xi/|x|,i=1,2,3,L^{0}=1,\quad L^{i}=x^{i}/|x|,\,\,\,\,i=1,2,3,\quad\text{and}\quad\underline{L}^{0}=1,\quad\underline{L}^{i}=-x^{i}/|x|,\,\,\,\,i=1,2,3,

6 The weak null condition and asymptotic expansion of Einstein’s equation’s in wave coordinates

Let us now first describe the weak null condition. The results of this section appear in [L-R]. Consider the Cauchy problem for a system of nonlinear wave equations in three space dimensions:

(6.1) −           ui=Fi(u,u′,u′′),i=1,…,N,u=(u1,…,uN),-\,\,\hbox{\vrule\vbox to7.0pt{\hrule\hbox to7.0pt{\hfil}\vfil\hrule}\vrule}\,\,u_{i}\,\,=F_{i}(u,u^{\prime},u^{\prime\prime}),\qquad i=1,...,N,\qquad u=(u_{1},...,u_{N}),

where −□=−∂t2+∑j=13∂xj2-\square=-\partial_{t}^{2}+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_{x^{j}}^{2}. We assume that FF is a function of uu and its derivatives of the form

Here we used the summation convention over repeated indices. We assume that the initial data

(6.3) u⁡(0,x)=ε​u0​(x)∈C∞,ut​(0,x)=ε​u1​(x)∈C∞u(0,x)=\varepsilon u_{0}(x)\in C^{\infty},\quad u_{t}(0,x)=\varepsilon u_{1}(x)\in C^{\infty}

is small and decays fast as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty. We are going to determine conditions on the nonlinearity such that the equation (6.1) is compatible with the asymptotic expansion as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty and |x|∼t|x|\sim t

(6.4) u⁡(t,x)∼ε​U​(q,s,ω)/|x|, where q=|x|−t,s=ε​ln⁡|x|,ω=x/|x|,u(t,x)\sim\varepsilon U(q,s,\omega)/|x|,\quad\text{ where }\quad q=|x|-t,\,\,\,s=\varepsilon\ln{|x|},\,\,\,\omega=x/|x|,

for all sufficiently small ϵ>0\epsilon>0. The linear and some nonlinear wave equations allow for such an expansion with UU independent of ss and the next term decaying like ε/|x|2\varepsilon/|x|^{2}, see [H1, H2]. Substituting (6.4) into (6.1) and equating powers of order ε2/|x|2\varepsilon^{2}/|x|^{2} we see that

(6.5) 2​∂s∂qUi=Ai​m​nj​k​(ω)​(∂qmUj)​(∂qnUk),U|s=0=F0,2\partial_{s}\partial_{q}U_{i}=A_{i\,mn}^{jk}(\omega)(\partial_{q}^{m}U_{j})(\partial_{q}^{n}U_{k}),\qquad\quad U\big|_{s=0}=F_{0},

where

(6.6) Ai,m​nj​k​(ω)=∑|α|=m,|β|=nai,α​βj​k​ω^α​ω^β,where ​ω^=(−1,ω)and ​ω^α=ω^α1​…​ω^αkA_{i,mn}^{jk}(\omega)=\sum_{|\alpha|=m,|\beta|=n}{a_{i,\alpha\beta}^{jk}\hat{\omega}^{\alpha}\hat{\omega}^{\beta}},\qquad\text{where }\hat{\omega}=(-1,\omega)\quad\text{and }\hat{\omega}^{\alpha}=\hat{\omega}_{\alpha_{1}}...\hat{\omega}_{\alpha_{k}}

In fact, □u=−ε−1∂s∂q(ru)+angular derivatives\square u=-\varepsilon^{-1}\partial_{s}\partial_{q}(ru)+\text{angular derivatives} and ∂μ=ω^μ∂q+tangential derivatives\partial_{\mu}=\hat{\omega}_{\mu}\partial_{q}+\text{tangential derivatives}.

One can show that (6.1)-(6.3) has a solution as long as ε​log⁡t\varepsilon\log{t} is bounded, provided that ε>0\varepsilon>0 is sufficiently small and the solution of (6.5) exists up to that time, [J-K, H1, H2, L1, L2]. The only exception is the case Ai​00j​k≠0A^{jk}_{i00}\neq 0, which has shorter life span. In cases where the solution of (6.5) blows up it has been shown that solutions of (6.1)-(6.3) also break down in some finite time Tε≤eC/εT_{\varepsilon}\leq e^{C/\varepsilon}, [J1, H1, A1]. John’s example was

(6.7) □​u=ut​△​u\square u=u_{t}\,\triangle u

for which (6.5) is the Burger’s equation (2∂s−Uq∂q)Uq=0(2\partial_{s}-U_{\!q}\partial_{q})U_{\!q}=0, which is known to blow up. The equation

(6.8) □​u=ut2\square u=u_{t}^{2}

is another example where solutions blow up, for which (6.5) is ∂sUq=Uq2\partial_{s}U_{\!q}=U_{\!q}^{2}, that also blows up.

The null condition of [K2] is equivalent to

(6.9) Ai​m​nj​k​(ω)=0for all ​(i,j,k,m,n),ω∈𝕊2.A_{i\,mn}^{jk}(\omega)=0\quad\text{for all }(i,j,k,m,n),\,\,\omega\in{\mathbb{S}}^{2}.

The results of [C1], [K2] assert that (6.1)-(6.3) has global solutions for all sufficiently small initial data, provided that the null condition is satisfies. In this case the asymptotic equation (6.5) trivially can be solved globally. Moreover, similar to the linear case, its solutions approach a limit as s→∞s\!\to\!\infty and the solutions of (6.1)-(6.3) decay like solutions of linear equations. A typical example of an equation satisfying the null condition is

(6.10) □​u=ut2−|∇xu|2\square u=u_{t}^{2}-|\nabla_{x}u|^{2}

There is however a more general class of nonlinearities for which solutions of (6.5) do not blow up:

We say that a system (6.1) satisfies the weak null condition if the solutions of the corresponding asymptotic system (6.5) exist for all ss and if the solutions together with its derivatives grow at most exponentially in ss for all initial data decaying sufficiently fast in qq.

Under the weak null condition assumption solutions of (6.5) satisfy the equation (6.1) up to terms of order ε2/|x|3−C​ε\varepsilon^{2}\!/|x|^{3-C\varepsilon}\!\!, but need only decay like ε/|x|1−C​ε\varepsilon/|x|^{1-C\varepsilon}\!\!. An example of the equation satisfying the weak null condition is given by

(6.11) □​u=u​△​u\square u=u\triangle u

In [L2] it was proven that (6.11) have small global solutions in the spherically symmetric case and recently [A3] established this result without the symmetry assumption. The equation (6.11) appears to be similar to (6.7) but a closer look shows that the corresponding asymptotic equation:

(6.12) (2∂s−U∂q)Uq=0(2\partial_{s}-U\partial_{q})U_{q}=0

has global solutions growing exponentially in ss, see [L2]. The system

(6.13) □​u=vt2,□​v=0\square u=v_{t}^{2},\qquad\square v=0

is another example that satisfies the weak null condition. The equation (6.13) appears to resemble (6.8). The system however decouples:  vv satisfies a linear homogeneous equation and given vv we have a linear inhomogeneous equation for uu, and global existence follows. The corresponding asymptotic system is

(6.14) ∂s∂qU=(∂qV)2,∂s∂qV=0\partial_{s}\partial_{q}U=(\partial_{q}V)^{2},\qquad\partial_{s}\partial_{q}V=0

The solution of the second equation in (6.14) is independent of ss: Vq=Vq​(q,ω)V_{q}=V_{q}(q,\omega) and substituting this into the first equation we see that Uq​(s,q,ω)=s​Vq​(q,ω)2U_{q}(s,q,\omega)=sV_{q}(q,\omega)^{2} so ∂u\partial u only decays like |x|−1​ln⁡|x||x|^{-1}\ln{|x|}.

We show below that the Einstein vacuum equations in wave coordinates satisfy the weak null condition, i.e. that the corresponding asymptotic system (6.5) admits global solutions. In fact, each of the quadratic nonlinear terms in the Einstein equations is either of the type appearing in (6.10), (6.11) or (6.13).

Theorem 6.1.

We now state the global Sobolev inequality, which is due to S. Klainerman [K1].

The following inequality holds for an arbitrary smooth function ϕ\phi.

10 Decay estimates for the wave equation on a curved space time

In this section we will derive some basic estimates for the scalar wave equation on a curved background. The results will require some weak assumptions on the metric gg, which will be easily verified in the case of a metric satisfying the reduced Einstein equations.

We consider the reduced scalar wave equation:

12 Estimates from the wave coordinate condition

In previous sections we have shown that one only needs to control certain components of the metric in order to establish decay estimates for solutions of the reduced wave equation. In this section we will see that the wave coordinate condition allows one to estimate precisely those components in terms of tangential derivatives or higher order terms with better decay better. Recall that the wave coordinate condition can be written in the form

(12.1) ∂μ(gμ​ν​|detg|)=0\partial_{\mu}\Big(g^{\mu\nu}\sqrt{|\det{g}|}\Big)=0

We have the following decomposition

gμ​ν​|detg|=(mμ​ν+Hμ​ν)​(1−12​tr​H+O⁡(H2))g^{\mu\nu}\sqrt{|\det{g}|}=\big(m^{\mu\nu}+H^{\mu\nu}\big)\big(1-\frac{1}{2}\text{tr}H+O(H^{2})\big)

where Hα​β=gα​β−mα​βH^{\alpha\beta}=g^{\alpha\beta}-m^{\alpha\beta}, hα​β=gα​β−mα​βh_{\alpha\beta}=g_{\alpha\beta}-m_{\alpha\beta}. Recall also that gα​βg^{\alpha\beta} is the inverse of gα​βg_{\alpha\beta} and Hα​β=−mμ​α​mν​β​hμ​ν+O⁡(h2)H^{\alpha\beta}=-m^{\mu\alpha}m^{\nu\beta}h_{\mu\nu}+O(h^{2}). Therefore we obtain the following expression for the wave coordinate condition:

we obtain:

13 Estimates for the inhomogeneous terms

In this section we will show that the inhomogeneous terms of the reduced Einstein equations can be estimated in terms of tangential derivatives, for which we have better decay estimates, or tangential components which in turn can be expressed, using the wave coordinate condition, in terms of tangential derivatives and lower order terms. Recall that according to Lemma 3.2 the symmetric two tensor hμ​ν=gμ​ν−mμ​νh_{\mu\nu}=g_{\mu\nu}-m_{\mu\nu} verifies the reduced Einstein equations of the form:

□~g​hμ​ν=Fμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h),\displaystyle\widetilde{\square}_{g}h_{\mu\nu}=F_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h),
(13.1) Fμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h)=P⁡(∂μh,∂νh)+Qμ​ν​(∂h,∂h)+Gμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h),\displaystyle F_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h)=P(\partial_{\mu}h,\partial_{\nu}h)+Q_{\mu\nu}(\partial h,\partial h)+G_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h),
(13.2) P⁡(∂μk,∂νp)=14​∂μtr​k​∂νtr​p−12​∂μkα​β​∂νpα​β,\displaystyle P(\partial_{\mu}k,\partial_{\nu}p)=\frac{1}{4}\partial_{\mu}\text{tr}k\,\partial_{\nu}\text{tr}p-\frac{1}{2}\partial_{\mu}k^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\nu}p_{\alpha\beta},

Here Q​μ​νQ{\mu\nu} are linear combinations of the null-forms and Gμ​ν​(h)​(∂h,∂h)G_{\mu\nu}(h)(\partial h,\partial h) is a quadratic form in ∂h\partial h with coefficients that are smooth functions of hh and vanishing at h=0h=0.

Lemma 13.1.

14 The decay estimates for Einstein’s equations

In this section we will establish the improved decay estimates for Einstein’s equations. Our strategy is to use the weak decay estimates, obtained from the assumed energy bounds, to prove sharper decay estimates and then to recover the energy bounds in the next section.

Theorem 14.1.

Suppose that for some 0<γ≤1/20<\gamma\leq 1/2

(14.1) |∂ZIh|≤Cε(1+t+|q|)−1/2−γ(1+|q|)−1/2−γ,|I|≤N/2+4,\displaystyle|\partial Z^{I}h|\leq C\varepsilon(1+t+|q|)^{-1/2-\gamma}(1+|q|)^{-1/2-\gamma},\qquad|I|\leq N/2+4,
(14.2) |ZI​h|≤C​ε​(1+t)−1,q=1,|I|≤N/2+4\displaystyle|Z^{I}h|\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1},\qquad q=1,\qquad|I|\leq N/2+4

hold for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T. Then for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T we have

(14.3) |ZIh|≤Cε(1+t+|q|)−1/2−γ(1+|q|)1/2−γ,|I|≤N/2+4,\displaystyle|Z^{I}h|\leq C\varepsilon(1+t+|q|)^{-1/2-\gamma}(1+|q|)^{1/2-\gamma},\qquad|I|\leq N/2+4,
(14.4) |∂¯ZIh|≤Cε(1+t+|q|)−3/2−γ(1+|q|)1/2−γ,|I|≤N/2+3.\displaystyle|\overline{\partial}Z^{I}h|\leq C\varepsilon(1+t+|q|)^{-3/2-\gamma}(1+|q|)^{1/2-\gamma},\qquad|I|\leq N/2+3.

Assume also that hh satisfies the wave coordinate condition. Then for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T we have

(14.5) |∂h|L​𝒯+|​∂Z​h|L​L≤C​ε​(1+t)−1−2​γ,and|h|L​𝒯+|​Z​h|L​L≤C​ε​(1+t)−1​(1+|q|).|\partial h|_{L\cal T}+|\partial Zh|_{LL}\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1-2\gamma},\qquad\text{and}\qquad|h|_{L\cal T}+|Zh|_{LL}\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1}(1+|q|).

Furthermore if in addition hh satisfies Einstein’s equations then for ε\varepsilon sufficiently small and 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T we also have

(14.6) |∂h|𝒯𝒰≤C​ε​(1+t)−1,|h|𝒯𝒰≤C​ε​(1+t)−1​(1+|q|),\displaystyle|\partial h|_{\cal TU}\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1},\qquad|h|_{\cal TU}\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1}(1+|q|),
(14.7) |∂h|≤C​ε​(1+t)−1​ln⁡(2+t).\displaystyle|\partial h|\leq C\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1}\ln(2+t).

In general, there are constants MkM_{k}, CkC_{k} and εk>0\varepsilon_{k}>0 such that if ε≤εk\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{k} then for |I|=k≤N/2+2|I|=k\leq N/2+2

(14.8) |∂ZI​h|≤Ck​ε​(1+t)−1+Mk​ε,and|ZI​h|≤Ck​ε​(1+t)−1+Mk​ε​(1+|q|)|\partial Z^{I}h|\leq C_{k}\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1+M_{k}\varepsilon},\qquad\text{and}\qquad|Z^{I}h|\leq C_{k}\varepsilon(1+t)^{-1+M_{k}\varepsilon}(1+|q|)
Remark 14.2.

We remind the reader that, as stated in the Remark 2.4, our estimates make no distinction between the tensors hh and H=−h+O⁡(h2)H=-h+O(h^{2}). In particular, one can directly verify that the conclusions of the theorem also hold for the tensor HH.

First we note that all the estimates (14.3)-(14.8) trivially follow from the assumptions (14.1)-(14.2) away from the light cone, thus the theorem is only useful in the region t/2≤|x|≤2​tt/2\leq|x|\leq 2t. The estimate (14.3) follows from integrating (14.1) from q=1q=1, where (14.2) hold. Similarly the second parts of (14.5), (14.6) and (14.8) follow from integrating the first and using (14.2). It follows from (14.3) and Lemma 7.2 that we have the better estimate (14.4) for the derivatives tangential to the outgoing Minkowski cones. The inequalities (14.5)-(14.8) for tangential derivatives certainly follow from (14.4), so it only remains to prove these estimates for a derivative transversal to the light cone.

The missing improved estimates for a (∂t−∂r)(\partial_{t}-\partial_{r}) derivative transversal to the light cones will be obtained, in the case of (14.5), from the wave coordinate condition, see section 12, and for (14.6)-(14.8), from integrating the reduced Einstein wave equations, see section 10. The estimates from the wave coordinate condition are easily obtained. In fact the first estimate in (14.5) follows directly from Lemma 12.1 using the estimates (14.1), (14.3) and (14.4) and the second estimate in (14.5) follows integrating the first from q=1q=1 where (14.2) holds. However, the wave coordinate condition does not give estimates for a transversal derivative of all components of the metric and the remaining components have to be controlled by integrating the wave equation expressed in polar coordinates. The estimates for the transversal derivative obtained from the wave coordinate condition rely on a decomposition of the metric with respect to the null frame. On the other hand, the estimates obtained from integrating the wave equation are based on a decomposition of the wave operator in terms of tangential derivatives and a transversal derivative.

14.1 Proof of (14.3) and (14.4)

For a fixed angular variable ω\omega we integrate in the radial direction and use (14.1) and (14.2)

(14.9) |ZI​h​(t,r,ω)|≤|ZI​h​(t,t+1,ω)|+∫rt+1|∂rZI​h​(t,ρ,ω)|​𝑑ρ≲C​ε1+t+∫rt+1C​ε​d​ρ(1+t+|t−ρ|)1/2+γ​(1+|t−ρ|)1/2+γ≲C​ε1+t+C​ε​(1+|t−r|)1/2+γ(1+t+r)1/2+γ|Z^{I}h(t,r,\omega)|\leq|Z^{I}h(t,t+1,\omega)|+\int_{r}^{t+1}|\partial_{r}Z^{I}h(t,\rho,\omega)|\,d\rho\\ \lesssim\frac{C\varepsilon}{1+t}+\int_{r}^{t+1}\frac{C\varepsilon\,d\rho}{(1+t+|t-\rho|)^{1/2+\gamma}(1+|t-\rho|)^{1/2+\gamma}}\lesssim\frac{C\varepsilon}{1+t}+\frac{C\varepsilon(1+|t-r|)^{1/2+\gamma}}{(1+t+r)^{1/2+\gamma}}

The estimate (14.3) now follows. By Lemma 7.2 and (14.3)

|∂¯​ZI​h|≲11+t+|q|​∑|J|≤|I|+1|ZJ​h|≲ε​(1+|q|)1/2−γ(1+t+|q|)3/2+γ|\overline{\partial}Z^{I}h|\lesssim\frac{1}{1+t+|q|}\sum_{|J|\leq|I|+1}|Z^{J}h|\lesssim\frac{\varepsilon(1+|q|)^{1/2-\gamma}}{(1+t+|q|)^{3/2+\gamma}}

which proves (14.4).

We have shown that all future inextendible causal geodesics X⁡(τ)X(\tau) exist for all values of the affine parameter τ∈[0,∞)\tau\in[0,\infty). This means that the constructed space-time is future causally geodesically complete. Next we establish that all future oriented causal geodesics escape to infinity.

Proposition 16.4.

(16.10) limτ→∞|X⁡(τ)|=∞\lim_{\tau\to\infty}|X(\tau)|=\infty
Proof.

The inequality (16.6) immediately gives the desired result for time-like geodesics. Recall that by Lemma 16.3 we have that x˙0​(τ)>0\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)>0 and thus x0​(τ)x^{0}(\tau) is monotonically increasing in τ\tau. We now argue by contradiction. Assume that for all τ≥0\tau\geq 0

|X⁡(τ)|≤C|X(\tau)|\leq C

for some potentially large constant CC. Then there exists a time t0t_{0} such that

t0=limτ→∞x0​(τ)t_{0}=\lim_{\tau\to\infty}x^{0}(\tau)

Set τ0\tau_{0} be the value of the proper time τ\tau for which t⁡(τ0)=t0−δt(\tau_{0})=t_{0}-\delta for some small constant δ\delta. Integrating the geodesic equation we obtain that for τ≥τ0\tau\geq\tau_{0}

(16.11) x˙0​(τ)=x˙0​(τ0)+∫τ0τ|Γ|​|x˙0|2​d​τ′≤x˙0​(τ0)+ε​∫t0−δtx˙0​d​t′≤x˙0​(τ0)+ε​δ​supτ0≤τ′≤τx˙0​(τ)\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)=\dot{x}^{0}(\tau_{0})+\int_{\tau_{0}}^{\tau}|\Gamma||\dot{x}^{0}|^{2}\,d\tau^{\prime}\leq\dot{x}^{0}(\tau_{0})+\varepsilon\int_{t_{0}-\delta}^{t}\dot{x}^{0}\,dt^{\prime}\leq\dot{x}^{0}(\tau_{0})+\varepsilon\delta\sup_{\tau_{0}\leq\tau^{\prime}\leq\tau}\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)

Thus for any τ≥τ0\tau\geq\tau_{0}

(16.12) x˙0​(τ)≤2​x˙0​(τ0)\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)\leq 2\dot{x}^{0}(\tau_{0})

Choosing a sequence of times τ0→∞\tau_{0}\to\infty such that x˙0​(τ0)→0\dot{x}^{0}(\tau_{0})\to 0 (such a sequence must exist, otherwise x0​(τ)→∞x^{0}(\tau)\to\infty) we infer from (16.12) that

x˙0​(τ)→0\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)\to 0

as τ→∞\tau\to\infty. We can then choose small constant c,δc,\delta such that t⁡(τ0)=t0−δt(\tau_{0})=t_{0}-\delta and

x˙0​(τ0)=c,x˙0​(τ)≤c\dot{x}^{0}(\tau_{0})=c,\qquad\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)\leq c

for all τ≥τ0\tau\geq\tau_{0}. Returning to (16.11) we see that

|x˙0​(τ)−c|≤ε​δ​c|\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)-c|\leq\varepsilon\delta c

Thus

x˙0​(τ)≥c2\dot{x}^{0}(\tau)\geq\frac{c}{2}

for all τ≥τ0\tau\geq\tau_{0} and we obtained contradiction. ∎
